Address read performance and scale deliberately: watch for the SELECT N+1 problem where a list query issues one query for IDs then a query per object (especially with foreign keys); a fully normalized schema prevents write corruption but its joins can be slow, so it is common to add denormalized views, read replicas, or caching, and once indexes are exhausted a denormalized read-optimized copy is reasonable because databases burn CPU on joins while single-key lookups are fastest; read-only stores scale out horizontally since reads have no concurrency limit (unlike writes needing locks), so if a complex store is hard to scale, ask whether a simpler read model would help.

Apply command-query separation so a function either modifies state or answers a question but never both (you should be able to ask whether the lights are on without flicking the switch): the Post/Redirect/Get pattern applies this at the web layer to avoid double-submits and broken bookmarks, and you should split read-only views from state-modifying command and event handlers into a separate module even if you do not go to full CQRS.
Test a view with at least one integration test whose setup goes through the public entrypoint, the message bus, so the test stays decoupled from any implementation detail of how the data is stored.

Recognize that view models can carry complex logic such as permissions and authorization and sometimes need extensive unit tests, so split a view builder that is easy to test with mocked data from a view fetcher.

Keep a denormalized read model up to date with event handlers that insert on allocation and delete on deallocation rather than database views or triggers that tie you to the database; a read model that fails to update is another case of events failing independently and can be rebuilt by replaying current write-side state through the update handler, and updating it through event handlers makes swapping its storage implementation (for example to Redis) easy while the same decoupled integration tests keep passing.

Use a Composition Root — a single bootstrap script — to perform manual dependency injection rather than loading the responsibility for passing dependencies to each handler onto the message bus (which would violate the single responsibility principle), composing a handler with its dependencies ahead of time using closures or functools.partial so it can be called later with them already injected, while noting that closures use late binding of variables which can confuse if a dependency is mutable.

Give the bootstrap script clear responsibilities: declare default dependencies while allowing overrides, perform one-time initialization such as ORM mapper start-up and logging configuration, inject dependencies into the handlers, and return the configured message bus; use its argument defaults as the single place for production defaults (defaulting a dependency to None when its construction has side effects), keep dependency injection in the single place of the handler functions, and reach for a real DI framework only when you need DI at multiple levels or have chained dependencies.

Build an external dependency as a proper adapter by defining its API with an abstract base class, implementing the real thing, building a fake for unit and handler tests, finding a less-fake version to run in your Docker environment, and testing that version — using an abstract base class for a complex multi-operation dependency but a plain function for a simple single-operation one — because once you have more than one adapter, passing dependencies around manually becomes painful without some form of dependency injection.

When improving an existing big ball of mud, first identify the problem you are solving — software too hard to change, unacceptable performance, or inexplicable bugs — because a clear goal helps prioritize the work and justify it; complex changes sell more easily when linked to feature work (the architecture tax), and you start breaking the ball apart by working out the system's use cases, treating each UI action or background job as one use case with an imperative name.

Create a single function or class per use case that orchestrates the work — starting its own transaction if needed, fetching data, checking preconditions, updating the domain model, and persisting changes as an atomic unit — accepting some duplication in use-case functions rather than having them call one another in a long chain, and pull data-access, orchestration, and I/O concerns out of the domain model up into these use-case functions while using abstractions to keep them unit-testable even when they perform I/O.

Avoid building a system where you dot your way through a connected object graph via the ORM: it is easy and convenient but each property access might trigger a database lookup, making performance hard to reason about.

Migrate a legacy system with the Strangler Fig pattern, building a new system around the edges of the old one and gradually intercepting and replacing functionality until the old system does nothing and can be switched off; move functionality with event interception (raise events for the system to replace, build a second system consuming them to build its own model, then replace the old), and when deploying an event-driven system start with a walking skeleton — a first production deployment that just logs its input — to force all the infrastructural questions early.

Configure the application through environment variables per the 12-factor manifesto so the same code runs on a developer machine, on containers, and across environments, centralizing access in a config module that uses functions rather than import-time constants; do not let that module become a dumping ground (keep values immutable, change them only via environment variables, and if you use a bootstrap script make it the only import site besides tests), and provide local-development defaults or fail hard on missing environment variables when a default would be insecure in production.

Keep packaging and build hygiene: in a Dockerfile install things in order of how frequently they change (system dependencies, then Python dependencies, then source) to maximize build-cache reuse, keep application source in an src folder installed with an editable pip install via a minimal setup.py, centralize common developer and CI commands in a Makefile (which as code stays less stale than documentation), and minimize the number of Docker images since splitting per code type usually costs more than it is worth.

Rely on decoupled infrastructure to make backends swappable: because infrastructure concerns are separated from the domain model and service layer, swapping the storage backend (for example from a database to CSV files) is just a matter of writing new Repository and Unit of Work classes while reusing all domain-layer and service-layer logic, since a CSV-backed repository can present the same in-memory-collection illusion as a database-backed one.

Apply the patterns carefully in Django, which is harder because its ORM has no classical-mapper equivalent so the ActiveRecord and domain model cannot be the same object and need a manual translation layer, and which suits easy CRUD but hinders once the app is non-CRUD (its admin becomes dangerous by bypassing complex state-change rules): in an existing Django app adopt Repository and Unit of Work mainly for faster tests and decoupling if migrating and the Service Layer when views duplicate, do DDD via fat models only while the app stays simple (extracting a domain layer between views/forms and models once fat models hit scalability limits), and put a logic module in every Django app from day one.

Follow Postel's Law, being liberal in what you accept and conservative in what you emit — strict when sending messages to other systems, lenient when receiving them — and do not over-validate opaque identifiers such as SKUs, order numbers, or phone numbers: treat them as strings so other systems can change their format freely, since their internal structure is not your system's business.

Follow the Tolerant Reader pattern: extract only the fields you care about, validate them minimally, ignore extra unknown fields, and resist sharing message definitions between systems, which keeps you robust as other systems change; this and Postel's approach suit event-based integration between services you control because they allow independent evolution, though a public internet-facing API may have good reason to be more conservative about the inputs it allows.

Validate at the edge so requests are known to be valid before the domain model or use-case handlers see them, keeping the domain free of defensive checks, because invalid data wandering through the system is a time bomb that does more damage the deeper it gets; the message bus is a good home for this cross-cutting validation, with entrypoints only receiving a message and reporting success or failure while the bus validates and routes and handlers focus on use-case logic, and since an invalid message usually leaves little to do but log and continue, count messages received, processed, skipped, and invalid and alert on spikes of bad ones.

Validate semantics — the meaningfulness of a message — at the message-handler or service layer using contract-based preconditions gathered in an ensure module, which keeps the main flow clean and declarative, and apply messages idempotently with a precondition that uses the same Unit of Work as the main logic (to avoid concurrency bugs), raising a SkipMessage for a message that cannot be processed but represents no incorrect behavior, such as a duplicate create.

Locate each type of validation in its right place — syntax on the message classes, semantics in the service layer or on the message bus, and pragmatics in the domain model where context-dependent business rules such as having enough stock naturally live — being clear about which of the three kinds you mean, and invest in declarative helpers for validation and preconditions because making this otherwise-boring code clean and easy to maintain pays off.
